examples.text: Вы решили почистить пятьдесят килограммов рыбы?
examples.trans: You decided to clean fifty kilograms of fish?

examples.text: Тут пять килограммов сгорело!
examples.trans: Five kilograms burned here!

examples.text: Дайте, пожалуйста, два килограмма яблок.
examples.trans: Give me two kilograms of apples, please.

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'chef' (head, leader, from Latin 'caput'); in Russian kitchen culture 'шеф' is the standard form of address for the executive head chef.

examples.text: Шеф, брат, возьми хорошую рыбу!
examples.trans: Chef, brother, take some good fish!

examples.text: Шеф, посмотрите, а что это?
examples.trans: Chef, look, what is this?

examples.text: Шеф, неужели это контрабанда?
examples.trans: Chef, could this really be contraband?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('we') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.text: Ну да, мы с Мишей женимся.
examples.trans: Well yes, Misha and I are getting married.

examples.text: Саша, мы разве не решили вопросы?
examples.trans: Sasha, didn't we settle all the questions?

examples.text: Вот, видишь, мы действительно заняты.
examples.trans: There, you see, we really are booked.

meanings.note: Everyday conversational Russian num meaning 'one', frequent in spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Шеф, мы нашли один камень утром.
examples.trans: Chef, we found one stone this morning.

examples.text: Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: Give me just one.

examples.text: У меня один брат.
examples.trans: I have one brother.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'stone', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Тимур, ты в драгоценных камнях разбираешься?
examples.trans: Timur, do you know about precious stones?

examples.text: Шеф, мы нашли один камень утром.
examples.trans: Chef, we found one stone this morning.

examples.text: Продам камни, а деньги поделим поровну.
examples.trans: I will sell the stones, and we will split the money equally.

meanings.note: Declinable neuter noun meaning 'morning', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Только утром из Якутии привезли.
examples.trans: They brought it from Yakutia just this morning.

examples.text: Помнишь, я утром рыбу брал?
examples.trans: Do you remember I took a fish this morning?

examples.text: Шеф, мы нашли один камень утром.
examples.trans: Chef, we found one stone this morning.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'and', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.

examples.text: А я решила отпраздновать здесь свадьбу.
examples.trans: And I decided to celebrate my wedding here.

examples.text: Слушай, ну не обижай её, а.
examples.trans: Listen, do not offend her, huh.

examples.text: Виктория Сергеевна, а что происходит?
examples.trans: Viktoriya Sergeyevna, what is going on?

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'in' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.text: Хотим отпраздновать в узком кругу.
examples.trans: We want to celebrate in a close circle.

examples.text: Сейчас посмотрю в нашем журнале.
examples.trans: I will look in our logbook right now.

examples.text: Вон в соседний ресторан продай.
examples.trans: Go sell it to the restaurant next door.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('maybe') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Может, поможешь?
examples.trans: Maybe you could help?

examples.text: Может, завтра.
examples.trans: Maybe tomorrow.

examples.text: Я думал, может, не примешь.
examples.trans: I thought maybe you wouldn't see me.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (root 'звонить'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to call', forming an aspectual pair with 'звонить'.

examples.text: Может, нам в полицию позвонить?
examples.trans: Maybe we should call the police?

examples.text: Может, позвонить Тимуру, пусть ещё привезёт?
examples.trans: Maybe we should call Timur and have him bring more?

examples.text: Просто Саша позвонила и попросила помочь.
examples.trans: Sasha simply called and asked for help.

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'timur', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Может, позвонить Тимуру, пусть ещё привезёт?
examples.trans: Maybe we should call Timur and have him bring more?

examples.text: Между прочим, это кража со взломом!
examples.trans: By the way, this is burglary with breaking and entering!

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('let') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Может, позвонить Тимуру, пусть ещё привезёт?
examples.trans: Maybe we should call Timur and have him bring more?

examples.text: Пусть строят.
examples.trans: Let them build.

examples.text: Пусть он придёт.
examples.trans: Let him come.

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (root 'везти'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to bring', forming an aspectual pair with 'привозить'.

examples.text: Только утром из Якутии привезли.
examples.trans: They brought it from Yakutia just this morning.

examples.text: Позже они не успеют привезти!
examples.trans: Later they will not make it in time to deliver!

examples.text: Может, позвонить Тимуру, пусть ещё привезёт?
examples.trans: Maybe we should call Timur and have him bring more?
